Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
Nothing good can happen to me anymore

vignette: Arjun was twenty-four when the encounter on the south side of the city ended with his face pressed into the damp asphalt, knees drawn tight against his ribs, hands cuffed behind his back. A steady drizzle had soaked through his shirt until his skin registered a precise, shivering chill that clung to him long after the patrol car lights faded. When he was finally released, it was a woman officer who approached his shoulder alone to explain the citation, her proximity leaving him frozen until he could stand and walk away. Over the following weeks, he found that thinking about the encounter brought a heavy, suffocating grief that made it difficult to breathe. His body began to mirror that original posture; when the memories surfaced, his shoulders curled inward, his knees pressed together, and his breath shallowed as if he were still being held down. When he thought of the event, the smell of wet wool and iron would sometimes rise in his throat, pulling him back to that exact moment on the pavement. He began to notice how his nervous system mapped the world in terms of that particular coldness. A draft from a subway vent, the condensation on a glass, even the temperature of a hand on his arm could send him into a quiet panic. He had come to believe that his physical reactions since the encounter proved he was a lousy coper, a conviction that settled heavily on his chest each morning. He started avoiding elevators with female colleagues, choosing the stairs instead. When his wife's friends visited, he would remain in the living room with the television on, steering conversations toward the weather or the news, certain that leaving her alone with any other woman would only invite the kind of suffocating stillness he had learned to dread. Over time, the avoidance of certain spaces and company settled into a quiet pattern. He was certain that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore; the editing work he once enjoyed, the quiet dinners, the plans he had made-all of it felt like standing in shallow water, watching things slip past without catching hold. At his job as an editor, the avoidance took shape in practical, unremarkable ways. He declined peer review sessions with the female senior editors, citing scheduling conflicts, and began leaving his office before the late-afternoon light shifted to match the temperature he remembered. He stopped taking phone calls in the glass-walled conference room where a woman once spoke to him on speakerphone. He told himself that nothing good could happen to him anymore, a belief that made him keep his curtains drawn and his phone on silent. He noticed the dissociation creeping in during long editing sessions; his eyes would remain fixed on a manuscript, but his awareness would thin, the desk and the keyboard would feel distant, and he would lose track of whether he was still in the room or somewhere else. He did not understand why his body kept returning to that pinned posture, or why the grief would rise so suddenly when he read a certain phrase, but he accepted the exhaustion as the cost of simply getting through the day. It was his wife who finally noticed how his hands trembled when the temperature in the room dropped, and how he flinched when she reached for his shoulder. She pointed out the missed deadlines, the closed office door, the way he had stopped attending the community dinners they used to host. Arjun agreed to make an appointment, though he carried a quiet dread about what the therapist might ask him to remember. What he hoped for, beneath the fear, was a way to stop his body from bracing for a threat that had already passed, and to find a reason to turn the blinds back open again. He was ready to stop believing he was failing at his own life.
